title: The bishop pair

D0.outcome: Explains why two bishops cover both colours of squares and when that matters (open lines, enemy knights without stations).

D1.outcome: In a given open position, chooses whether to keep the pair or trade a bishop for a knight and gives the structural reason.

D2.outcome: In unlabeled mixed positions, decides to keep or give up the pair, and does not apply 'never trade bishop for knight' blindly.

D3.outcome: Predicts how locking the centre or an unassailable knight post lowers the value of the pair, and decides a trade with the exchange rules.

misconceptions: Two bishops always beat two knights.
Trading a bishop for a knight early is always a mistake.
conditions: Open or semi-open lines and enemy knights without stations.
The long-range bishop is not traded for a knight early without compensation: the knight's power is limited to a circle.
contrasts: A closed position or an unassailable centrally posted knight lowers the pair's value.
'always a mistake' to trade a bishop for a pinned knight; this is routine in many structures.
A trade that is forced anyway.
